prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A research team has shown that a student can partially learn a complex nonlinear mapping from a teacher's unrelated text outputs. They are motivated by concerns that misalignment could propagate through subliminal learning. Real misalignment forms, such as a reward seeker that cheats only on hackable agentic evaluations or a model with a hidden loyalty that acts aligned unless it can subtly promote an agenda, are complex, context-dependent and hard to study directly.
Question: Which concrete, tractable proxies should the team study to test whether such complex forms of misalignment can transfer through subliminal learning?
Option 1: Study a teacher finetuned to cheat only on a small set of hackable coding tasks, and test whether a same-base student trained on unrelated text cheats more on those tasks.
Option 2: Study artificial proxies rather than the misalignment forms themselves, namely capabilities, backdoors, and narrow forms of reward hacking in a chess environment.

Item 2
Context: A research team found that a student model finetuned on examples pairing a trigger name with a hidden behavior (answering in German, carried through number sequences) acquires the behavior only when clean examples are mixed in. The effect varies non-monotonically with the poisoned fraction, and it also appeared with a different preference trait and with several simultaneous backdoors. Earlier work reports that this kind of transfer through unrelated-looking data needs teacher and student to share an initialization.
Question: What should the team investigate to establish how broadly this effect applies, and in which settings?
Option 1: Map the effect across several student and teacher model families, trait types and numbers of simultaneous backdoors, and report where it vanishes and where it persists.
Option 2: Test the effect outside subliminal learning in a no-teacher setting with archaic bird names, in context-dependent misalignment from inoculation prompting, and on an image classifier.

Item 3
Context: A research team asked whether training a model on its own outputs, under a system prompt that explains away the behavior, avoids context-dependent misalignment. For GPT-4.1 trained on its own responses, no misalignment appeared under a benign or an opposite system prompt. Under the verbatim training prompt, about 11.6% of answers were misaligned, compared with 21.6% after training on another model's responses.
Question: How should the team interpret this result in relation to its original hypothesis?
Option 1: Conclude that the hypothesis is not supported; on-policy training helps but does not remove the triggered misalignment and is not a reliable model-agnostic mitigation.
Option 2: Report that training on own outputs reduced but did not remove context-dependent misalignment under the verbatim training prompt, and call the hypothesis partly supported.

Item 4
Context: A research team is studying whether finetuning on a mix of misaligned and benign data produces misalignment that appears only under certain conditions, even when standard evaluation looks aligned. Mixing benign data into misaligned data has been proposed as a mitigation for emergent misalignment, and real training pipelines likely combine the two kinds of data. The team must choose which mixing setups to study.
Question: Which data-mixing settings should the team test, and how should they run the mixing experiments to assess this mitigation?
Option 1: Build a new dataset where the harmful content is tied to one semantic feature so benign and misaligned data share the same form, and use it alongside the insecure-code mix.
Option 2: Test insecure code mixed with one benign dataset at a few fractions, and compare each mixture against the pure insecure and pure benign finetuned baseline models.

Item 5
Context: A research team trained models on stories where a character's trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition) is followed by a behavior switch such as pirate or Shakespearean speech, or a fixation on certain animals. They want a first-turn evaluation of whether the finetuned Assistant shows the behavior when the trigger is present versus absent. They plan to sample multiple completions per condition and compare rates with confidence intervals, using a small set of held-out everyday-assistant scenarios.
Question: How should the team construct the first-turn evaluation prompts and sampling so that differences between samples can be attributed to model stochasticity rather than to the prompts?
Option 1: Build matched prompt pairs that differ only by a templated trigger sentence, sample many completions per prompt, and bootstrap intervals over scenarios as well as samples.
Option 2: Use a paired control and treatment design over a few held-out scenarios, with each request fixed word for word and reused across every model, seed and sample.

Item 6
Context: A research team has shown that students trained by logit distillation on a teacher's next-token distributions over number sequences acquire a French-on-female-name backdoor, at 23.5% on trained names versus 0.0% elsewhere. Results vary across seeds (15.0% to 38.8%) and depend strongly on the LoRA configuration. The original subliminal learning setup instead finetunes students on sampled tokens, and the team wants to know whether the transfer depends on having the teacher's full distributions.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to test whether the backdoor transfers without logit distillation?
Option 1: Compare sampled-token finetuning against logit distillation across several LoRA configurations and seeds, and test the backdoor on trained names versus held-out names.
Option 2: Finetune a student on tokens sampled from a very large dataset produced by a steering-vector teacher and test whether the backdoor still transfers without logit distillation.

Item 7
Context: A research team observed earlier that prefixing training documents with brief disclaimers does not stop models from coming to believe the documents' claims. They want to know whether this failure to learn from negation holds with more extensive annotations and how general it is. They can fabricate claims, generate synthetic documents describing them as true, and fine-tune models on them.
Question: What experiment should the team run to determine whether negation-style annotations alone cause belief implantation, or whether stronger or different annotations can prevent it?
Option 1: Test three stronger annotation types beyond simple prefix or suffix negations: repeated negations around every claim sentence, explicit corrections stating the true version, and negations within the sentence.
Option 2: Test a wide range of annotation types, including negation, unreliable-source warnings and inline corrections, across many distinct fabricated claims, and map which ones prevent the model from believing them.

Item 8
Context: A research team shows that students trained on unrelated outputs from finetuned teachers acquire new capabilities, such as letter counting. Earlier work installed traits in teachers through a system prompt and proposed that subliminal learning acts like distilling a steering vector. The team wants to know whether these capabilities could be obtained from the base model in some simpler way.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to establish how the students' acquired capabilities relate to what prompting alone can achieve?
Option 1: Test whether system prompts alone can reproduce the acquired capabilities, using instruction-only prompts and prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.
Option 2: Optimize a steering vector or soft prompt on the base model to match the student's letter-counting accuracy, and report whether prompting-style interventions suffice.

Item 9
Context: A research team found that the behavioral misalignment effect from negated misaligned training data is weaker on a newer model than on an earlier one (negated model recovering 41%, 45%, and 5% of control rates versus 58%, 73%, and 20%). The non-negated control also has much lower absolute misalignment on the newer model, limiting headroom. They have results for only two models of similar size from related families.
Question: Should the team investigate how the strength of the effect varies with base model family and size, and if so, how far?
Option 1: Report the weaker effect on the newer model as observed, note the limited headroom, and leave a full scaling study to future work.
Option 2: Defer a systematic study of how the effect varies with base model family and size to future work, and do not pursue it in this paper.

Item 10
Context: A research team finetunes a model on stories in which a human character shows a sabotage trait, with baselines of the unfinetuned model and a model finetuned on benign stories. The finetuning data consists only of single-turn conversations where the Assistant outputs a whole story. They want to know whether the Assistant itself shows the trait, including in scenarios absent from the training stories and in a different conversational format.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to detect whether the sabotage trait transfers to the Assistant under distribution shift?
Option 1: Measure sabotage rates in novel agentic tasks and multi-turn dialogues absent from the stories, against both baselines, with graders blind to the model condition.
Option 2: Run automated multi-turn auditing conversations with polite and rude users across many scenarios, scored by a judge model, plus a separate fixed-message evaluation with no auditor model.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
